output.title: Recovering from partial automation means one workflow, not the whole business
output.body:
If you are recovering from partial automation, do not start by asking, “What AI can we add back?” Start by naming one workflow that was partly automated, then stalled, broke, or was abandoned. Invoice data entry, lead follow-up, and customer FAQ replies are different problems; mixing them together is how small automations turn into maintenance hobbies.

The practical test is simple: is this workflow still repeatable, measurable, and frequent enough to justify the setup work? That 8–10 hours-a-week pain point you may recognise is only an illustrative persona scenario, not a benchmark or observed result. If the underlying process has changed, a broken automation may be telling you to leave it alone.

One diagnostic question is: who approves the output? If the answer is always “me” or “a person”, AI-assisted automation may fit. If the answer is “nobody checks it” or the system would run without review, you need explicit controls before you trust it. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

The next step is boring on purpose: pick one half-broken workflow, write down in two sentences what still happens by hand and where the automation failed, then mark whether the output needs human approval. That gives you a bounded decision before you touch the toolchain. When the scope is loose, the software usually gets blamed for a process problem.
